draft.title: The printing press
card: Before about 1450, books in Europe were copied by hand. This was slow and costly, so few people owned books.
Around 1450, Johannes Gutenberg of Mainz, in what is now Germany, built a press using movable type. Metal letters could be set in a frame, inked and pressed onto paper, then reused for the next page.
Presses could make many copies of a book much faster and more cheaply. Books and ideas spread across Europe, and more people learned to read.
Printing helped Reformation ideas reach many readers. Scientists could also share their findings in print and others could check them.
draft.remember: Cheap, fast printing let ideas travel further, which helped the Reformation and science.

a.q: What made Gutenberg's press different from copying books by hand?
opts: Reusable metal letters let many copies be made quickly
It let each scribe copy a book with more skill
It allowed books to be written only in Latin
It made paper from cloth for the first time
a.why: Movable type could be set, inked and pressed again and again, so copies were quicker and cheaper. Better scribes would still copy one page at a time by hand, so skill did not change the speed.
a.clue: Think about what could be reused for each new page.

b.q: In the 1500s, a town in Germany gets a printing press. Why would this help a new religious idea spread beyond the town?
opts: Cheap printed copies could reach many readers far away
Printers were able to check that every idea was true
Fewer people needed to read for the idea to spread
Hand copying became faster than printing
b.why: Printing made many copies cheaply, so writing could travel to readers in other places. The press did not check whether ideas were true, so it spread good and bad ideas alike.
b.clue: Focus on how many copies could be made and how cheaply.

a.best: Reusable metal letters let many copies be made quickly

b.best: Cheap printed copies could reach many readers far away
